teach.title: The ending says who

notice.ask: Which verb in each sentence means 'you' are doing it, and what last letter do the two share?

teach.say: A Latin verb carries its own subject in its last letters: **the person endings (I / you / he / we / you all / they on the verb)**. One verb, three people, no extra word needed: *cantō* I sing, *cantās* you sing, *cantat* he or she sings.

check.ask: Which of the three verbs here means 'you sing'?

teach.title: The singular three: -ō, -s, -t
teach.say: On a verb of the first conjugation (the -āre family) the singular endings are *-ō* (I), *-s* (you, one person) and *-t* (he, she, it): *cantō, cantās, cantat*. The *-ā-* in front is not part of the ending; it belongs to the verb's own family.

check.ask: Fill the three singular cells of cantāre: I, you, he/she.

teach.title: The plural three: -mus, -tis, -nt
teach.say: More than one: *-mus* (we), *-tis* (you all), *-nt* (they) — *cantāmus, cantātis, cantant*. *-mus* and *-tis* are easy to hear. *-nt* is only two letters and is the one that slips past: *cantant* is they sing, where *cantat* is he sings.

check.ask: Fill the three plural cells of cantāre: we, you all, they.

teach.title: The vowel in front belongs to the verb
teach.say: The six endings never change; the vowel before them does. *cantā-s*, *vidē-s*, *leg-i-s*, *audī-s* are all 'you'. So *videt* and *legit* are both 'he', although one shows *-et* and the other *-it*: take the *-t* off and what is left is the verb, not the person.

check.ask: legit and videt: what person and number is each, and how do you know?

teach.title: -unt and -iunt are still 'they'
teach.say: Before *-nt* the third and fourth families put a *-u-*: *legunt* they read, *audiunt* they hear, *capiunt* they take. A 'they' can therefore end *-ant*, *-ent*, *-unt* or *-iunt*, and all four are the same *-nt* with a different vowel in front.

check.ask: audiunt: how many people are hearing, and which letters tell you?

teach.title: One or many: -t against -nt
teach.say: The commonest slip is reading *-nt* as *-t*. *canis lātrat* is one dog barking; *ovēs lātrant* is sheep barking, and the *n* is the whole difference. The subject noun agrees with it, so the two always confirm each other — and when the subject is *ego* or *vōs*, the ending must match that too: *ego taceō*, *vōs clāmātis*.

check.ask: Ego taceō, sed vōs ____ . Write the form of clāmāre that vōs needs.

core.text: A Latin verb carries its own subject in its ending: **the person endings (I / you / he / we / you all / they on the verb)**. *-ō* I, *-s* you, *-t* he / she / it, *-mus* we, *-tis* you all, *-nt* they. So *dormiō* is *I sleep*, *dormīs* *you sleep*, then *dormit, dormīmus, dormītis, dormiunt*. Between stem and ending sits the conjugation's vowel: *clāmā-s, rīdē-s, dīc-i-s, audī-s*; the 3rd and 4th conjugations have *-u-* before *-nt* (*dīcunt, faciunt, dormiunt*). Latin name: dēsinentiae persōnālēs āctīvae.
Person is who is talking: first person = the speaker (I, we), second = the listener (you), third = anyone else.
-ō, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt; the vowel in front belongs to the conjugation.

Each active ending has a passive twin: *-ō / -or*, *-s / -ris*, *-t / -tur*, *-mus / -mur*, *-tis / -minī*, *-nt / -ntur*: *laudō* I praise, *laudor* I am praised. A final *r* (or *-minī*) means the subject is on the receiving end, or the verb is a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks).

more.text: Because the ending says who, *ego* and *tū* appear only for emphasis. The 1st conjugation drops its *a* before *-ō*: *clāmā-re* but *clām-ō*. In the imperfect, the pluperfect, the 3rd- and 4th-conjugation future and every subjunctive the first person ends in *-m* instead of *-ō*: *eram, dīxeram, dīcam, dīcerem*. The 1st and 2nd conjugations keep *-ō* in the future, as does the future perfect (*amābō, ībō, dīxerō*), and the perfect has its own *-ī* (*dīxī*).

The learner's notes (week 15): the endings are *-ō / -m, -(i)s, -(i)t, -(i)mus, -(i)tis, -(u)nt*; the bracketed vowel appears where the stem ends in a consonant (*frang-is, frang-imus, frang-itis*) and not after *a-, e-* and *i-*stems (*ambulā-s, tenē-mus, audī-tis*); in the present indicative only *-ō* is used for *I*, and *a-*stems drop their *a* before it (*ambul-ō*) because two open vowels are hard to say together. The nominative pronouns *ego, tū, is* are redundant and mark emphasis, as English does with the voice, so *ambulō* is far commoner than *ego ambulō*.

Ørberg (chapter XV): persōna prīma *rīdeō rīdēmus*, secunda *rīdēs rīdētis*, tertia *rīdet rīdent*; *clāmō clāmāmus, dīcō dīcimus, faciō facimus, audiō audīmus*; and beside them *esse* (*sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*), *īre* (*eō, īs, it, īmus, ītis, eunt*) and *posse* (*possum, potes, potest, possumus, potestis, possunt*).
English has to put *I, you, he* in front; Latin changes the end of the verb instead.
Look at the last letter: *-ō* is the speaker, *-s* the one spoken to, *-t* somebody else.
